procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated the 27th May 1954 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 158 of 1953, which dismissed the appellant's appeal and confirmed his conviction and sentence.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta. He appealed to the Calcutta High Court, which dismissed the appeal. He then filed a petition for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. A Division Bench of the High Court (Chief Justice and Mr. Justice S. C. Lahiri) allowed the petition and ordered that a certificate for leave to appeal under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution may be drawn up.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the Calcutta High Court granted a certificate for leave to appeal under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court questioned the High Court's jurisdiction to grant such a certificate on what it considered to be a question of fact. The appellant also urged the Supreme Court to exercise its discretion and grant special leave to appeal under article 136(1) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether a High Court has the jurisdiction under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court on a mere question of fact.

facts: The Calcutta High Court granted a certificate for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution.

The Chief Justice of the High Court, in an elaborate judgment, acknowledged that the case involved a "question of fact" but granted the certificate because he had misgivings about whether the appellant had received a full and fair trial and felt the case deserved further consideration.
law: Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution allows a High Court to certify that a criminal case is a "fit one for appeal" to the Supreme Court.

Article 136(1) of the Constitution grants the Supreme Court a special and discretionary jurisdiction to grant leave to appeal in any case, including those involving questions of fact, particularly in instances of gross miscarriage of justice or when findings are shocking to the judicial conscience.
application: The Supreme Court ruled that a High Court has no jurisdiction to grant a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) on a mere question of fact.
The Court reasoned that the purpose of this certificate is not to convert the Supreme Court into a "Court of Appeal on facts."
The High Court's feeling that a fair trial was not held or its inability to remedy the situation is not a valid justification for granting the certificate.
The power to intervene on questions of fact in exceptional circumstances (like a gross miscarriage of justice) is a special jurisdiction reserved for the Supreme Court under Article 136(1).

A High Court cannot "arrogate that function to itself." The proper course for a High Court in such a situation is to refuse the certificate and advise the parties to directly petition the Supreme Court to invoke its special jurisdiction under Article 136(1).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court has no jurisdiction to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal under Article 134(1)(c) on a mere question of fact. It held that the certificate issued by the Calcutta High Court was wrongly granted and was, therefore, "no certificate at all."

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution can be blamed for the lacuna in the defence's case for not adducing evidence in support of its own contentions.

facts: The appellant (the accused) was convicted of possessing a stolen car.
The prosecution presented evidence, including an expert witness, to prove its case.
The appellant argued that certain documents on the record, if properly considered, would have demolished the prosecution's case.
However, the appellant did not formally adduce this evidence in his defense during the trial.
law: The prosecution has the burden to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
An accused person is not required to lead any evidence.
However, if the prosecution successfully establishes its case, it is the duty of the accused to adduce evidence to support their specific defense contentions.
application: The Court found that the prosecution had successfully established its case through the evidence it presented.
At that point, the Court reasoned it was the "bounden duty" of the appellant to present evidence to support his defense if he wished to prove it.
The Court stated that if the appellant failed to adduce evidence that could have potentially demolished the prosecution's case, he had "only to thank himself for it."
The Court explicitly held that the prosecution could not be blamed for this "lacuna" or gap in the defense's case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected this argument, deciding that the accused, and not the prosecution, is to be blamed for the lacuna in the defense's case. The Court reasoned that once the prosecution establishes its case, the responsibility to adduce evidence in support of any defense contentions falls upon the accused. The prosecution cannot be held responsible for the defense's failure to do so.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a High Court has the jurisdiction under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court on a mere question of fact.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position, supported by the High Court Chief Justice who granted the certificate, was that a certificate could be granted if there was a feeling that a 'full and fair trial' had not been held, entitling the petitioner to have their case further considered by the Supreme Court, even if it involved questions of fact.
respondent_arguments: A High Court cannot arrogate to itself the special jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136(1).
A High Court has no jurisdiction to grant a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) on a mere question of fact, even if it feels helpless to redress a grievance or suspects a miscarriage of justice.
In such cases, the High Court should refuse the certificate and advise the parties to approach the Supreme Court directly under its special jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution can be blamed for the lacuna in the defence's case for not adducing evidence in support of its own contentions.
appellant_arguments: There were documents on record (an application for car registration and a police report) which, if considered, would have been sufficient to demolish the prosecution's case.
The failure to fully consider this evidence meant the trial was not 'full and fair', implying a flaw for which the conviction should be overturned.
respondent_arguments: While the prosecution must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, it is the 'bounden duty' of the appellant to adduce evidence to support their own defence.
If the defence fails to present its evidence, it has only itself to thank.
The prosecution cannot be blamed for a lacuna or gap in the defence's case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court has no jurisdiction under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to grant a certificate for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on a mere question of fact; a certificate granted on such grounds is invalid.
obiter: The Supreme Court possesses special jurisdiction under Article 136(1) of the Constitution to intervene in cases of gross miscarriage of justice, a departure from legal procedure that vitiates the trial, or on findings of fact that are shocking to the judicial conscience.
An accused who fails to adduce evidence in support of their contentions is to be blamed for any resulting lacuna in the defence, not the prosecution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A High Court has no jurisdiction under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal on a mere question of fact, even if it has misgivings that a full and fair trial was not held. Such a certificate is invalid, as the High Court cannot arrogate to itself the special jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136(1). Furthermore, while the prosecution must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, it is the bounden duty of the accused to adduce evidence to support their own defence, and the prosecution cannot be blamed for any lacuna resulting from the defence's failure to do so.
legal_tests_applied: A certificate of fitness for appeal under Article 134(1)(c) cannot be granted on a mere question of fact.

The Supreme Court's special jurisdiction to intervene under Article 136(1) is reserved for cases of gross miscarriage of justice, a departure from legal procedure that vitiates the whole trial, or findings of fact that are shocking to the judicial conscience.

In a criminal trial, the prosecution has the burden to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, but it is the 'bounden duty' of the accused, if they wish to prove their defence, to adduce evidence in support of their contentions.
why_appellant_lost: The certificate for appeal granted by the High Court was invalid ('no certificate at all') because it was granted on a question of fact, which is outside the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 134(1)(c).

The High Court Chief Justice's feeling that a 'full and fair trial' had not been held was not a valid justification for granting the certificate, as the mere disability of the High Court to remedy a perceived injustice does not empower it to pass the matter to the Supreme Court on facts.
It was the 'bounden duty of the appellant if he wanted to prove his defence to adduce evidence in support of his contentions,' and having failed to do so, 'he had only to thank himself for it.'
The appellant could not blame the prosecution for the 'lacuna' in his own defence case, which arose from his failure to present evidence that he claimed would have demolished the prosecution's case.
why_respondent_won: The High Court has no jurisdiction to grant a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) on a mere question of fact; in such cases, it should refuse the certificate and advise the parties to approach the Supreme Court under its special jurisdiction.
A High Court cannot arrogate the special jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136(1) to itself simply because it feels helpless to redress a grievance or suspects a miscarriage of justice.
The prosecution cannot be blamed for the defence's failure to adduce evidence in support of its own contentions.
policy_considerations: Allowing High Courts to grant certificates on questions of fact would improperly convert the Supreme Court 'into a Court of Appeal on facts.'
A High Court cannot arrogate the special function and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136(1) to itself; this maintains the distinct jurisdictional hierarchy between the courts.
If an accused does not take counsel and put forward a defence as they should have, the blame lies with the defence, not the prosecution or the trial court.
